concepts.title: Map Projection: Need, Properties and Classification
concepts.definition: A map projection is the systematic drawing of the parallels and meridians of the globe on a flat surface, unavoidable because a sphere cannot be flattened without distortion; projections are classified by developing surface into cylindrical, conical and zenithal or azimuthal families, and by preservation into equal area, true shape and equidistant types.
concepts.textbook_ref: No projection can keep area, shape and distance all true at once, so each projection is chosen for the purpose of the map.

concepts.title: Types of Projections and Their Suitability
concepts.definition: Zenithal projections suit polar areas, cylindrical projections like Mercator suit equatorial regions and navigation with true directions, conical projections with one or two standard parallels suit mid latitude countries, and Bonne's projection suits equal area mapping of a continent.
concepts.textbook_ref: Mercator keeps directions true with growing area towards poles, while Sanson-Flamsteed and Bonne keep areas true for distribution maps.

concepts.title: Drawing and Choosing Projections for Map Making
concepts.definition: Drawing a projection means constructing the graticule of parallels and meridians by geometry from the chosen properties, and the cartographer picks the projection after weighing the area to be mapped, its latitudinal position and the purpose of the map.
concepts.key_idea: For example, a zenithal equidistant projection serves a polar map, a polyconic suite serves India's topographical sheets and Mercator serves ocean route charts.
